title: Human Spatial Behavior
review_question: To critically evaluate past approaches and recent developments in the field of human spatial behavior, emphasizing theoretical drifts and the need for sociological input.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: The review emphasizes theoretical drifts that have directed research on human spatial behavior and limits discussion to work related to social and psychological variables in association with the spatial dimension.

findings.antecedent: Abnormal spatial situations (e.g., close individual distances, territorial invasions, overcrowded conditions)
findings.consequent: Specific kinds of responses (e.g., aggression, psychological stress)
findings.quote: There is no consistent evidence, however, that abnormal spatial situations elicit specific kinds of responses among humans.

findings.antecedent: Cultural background (e.g., 'contact' vs. 'noncontact' cultures, subcultures)
findings.consequent: Appropriate interpersonal distances and densities
findings.quote: persons from different cultures vary in the interpersonal distances and densities that they consider to be appropriate.

findings.antecedent: Environmental design (e.g., 'good' vs. 'bad' design, sociopetal/sociofugal arrangements, forced contact, shared space)
findings.consequent: Human attitudes, actions, social interaction, community spirit, well-being, crime rates
findings.quote: the physical characteristics of a setting per se have a large influence on our attitudes and actions

findings.antecedent: Physical distances among individuals and high density per se
findings.consequent: Specific individual responses
findings.quote: Physical distances among individuals and high density per se were poor predictors of specific individual responses

findings.antecedent: Persons' perceptions of the situation (e.g., imagined ongoing activity, environmental context)
findings.consequent: What is considered overcrowded or physically too close
findings.quote: persons' perceptions of the situation had significant impacts upon what was considered overcrowded or physically too close.

findings.antecedent: Perceived crowding
findings.consequent: Poorer academic performance and health
findings.quote: perceived crowding was related to poorer academic performance and health among university students.

findings.antecedent: High urban density and close daily contacts
findings.consequent: Nervous system overload
findings.quote: urban life as a situation in which individuals typically had too many daily contacts at very close distances with others... led to "overloading" the nervous system.

findings.antecedent: Stimulus overload (from high density)
findings.consequent: Social withdrawal (limiting involvement in associations, avoiding others)
findings.quote: The principal adaptations were referred to as "social withdrawal," or attempts by individuals to limit their involvement in some associations and totally avoid others.

findings.antecedent: Crowding and close spatial proximity
findings.consequent: High 'attentional demand' leading to 'cognitive fatigue' and aftereffects (e.g., deficits in task performance, less attention to postcrowding social stimuli)
findings.quote: Density and close spatial proximity are said to lead to high "attentional demand," since individuals must monitor a good deal of potentially threatening stimuli, and this results in "cognitive fatigue" and various aftereffects

findings.antecedent: High densities
findings.consequent: Specialized withdrawal (conserving energies by attending to rewarding encounters and avoiding neutral/harmful interactions)
findings.quote: individuals learn to conserve energies by attending to more rewarding encounters and avoiding neutral or potentially harmful interactions.

findings.antecedent: Lack of predictability and controllability (of environmental stressors like noise)
findings.consequent: Stress response and behavioral/psychological deficits (e.g., decreased abilities in completing puzzles)
findings.quote: it was the lack of predictability and controllability of the experience that caused a stress response

findings.antecedent: Perceived control (even without actual control)
findings.consequent: Behavioral responses to environmental stressors
findings.quote: the mere perception of control over the noise stimulus (without actual control during the situation) exerted a significant influence over behavioral responses to the situation.

findings.antecedent: Crowding (as a situation beyond individual control)
findings.consequent: Poor task performance (aftereffects of stress exposure), powerlessness, 'learned helplessness'
findings.quote: Crowding has recently been viewed as a situation in which individuals are confronted with environmental circumstances beyond their control.

findings.antecedent: Social meanings attached to environments (through interaction and socialization)
findings.consequent: Human spatial responses
findings.quote: The social meanings that people attach to environments through their interactions and ongoing socialization thus would play an important role in determining human spatial responses

findings.antecedent: Disagreement on space allocation (e.g., within nonrelated household groups)
findings.consequent: Interpersonal tension, role interference, psychological stress
findings.quote: Problems arise when those sharing a common space do not have the same views about how this resource should be allocated, since this could hinder the enactment of individually preferred roles.

findings.antecedent: Short supply of household space
findings.consequent: Role conflict, incomplete role performances, intrusions, blocking of desired role enactments
findings.quote: If there is not enough room or privacy to conduct desired roles alone and with others, competition for space use may occur.

findings.antecedent: Alteration of one nonverbal cue (e.g., interpersonal distance)
findings.consequent: Compensatory shifts along another dimension (e.g., eye contact) to maintain situational meaning
findings.quote: the alteration of one factor seemed to create shifts along another dimension (e.g. closer distances led to less eye contact, or vice versa).

findings.antecedent: Lack of needed privacy (personal space violations, territorial invasions, crowding) or inadequate social contact (low density, far interpersonal distances)
findings.consequent: Feelings of spatial inadequacy or isolation
findings.quote: the needed privacy is lacking (personal space violations, territorial invasions, and crowding) as there are situations in which inadequate social contact leads to feelings of isolation

findings.antecedent: Crowding
findings.consequent: Stress, leading to a chain reaction of behaviors, attitudes, and environmental manipulations, resulting in either adaptation/successful functioning or continued stress/malfunctioning
findings.quote: crowding leads to stress, which then sets off a chain reaction (e.g. behaviors, attitudes, environmental manipulations) by and within the individual.

findings.antecedent: Residential dissatisfaction
findings.consequent: Mobility, adjustments of residential structure, adjustments in family interaction, or attitudinal changes (environmental optimalization)
findings.quote: residential dissatisfaction can result in mobility, adjustments of the residential structure, adjustments in family interaction, or attitudinal changes.

synthesis_conclusions: Human spatial behavior is influenced by a complex interaction of spatial resources, temporal factors, social structure, and psychological phenomena.
Sociology has a relevant role in studying spatial activity, as space is a valuable resource with communicative roles in social life.
Individuals have high adaptive capacities and manipulate social and spatial variables to optimize rewards.
The field has matured beyond deterministic views and single-variable experimental studies, moving towards multivariate and longitudinal approaches.
Equilibrium theories offer a thorough theoretical and methodological way to investigate human spatial behavior, but should not assume balanced solutions or ignore social position.
evidence_gaps: Lack of sociological input in the study of human spatial behavior.
Insufficient research on spatial differentiation, ordering of activities, or social control of space through social mechanisms.
Lack of studies on the socialization of space use and the development of spatial meanings and subsequent responses.
Limited work on the 'antecedent variables' of spatial factors and behaviors.
Shortage of sociological methods, such as systematic large-scale surveys and longitudinal observations.
Need for proper empirical testing of subjective-crowding models and density-intensity theory.
Need for further clarification and testing of competing models for perceived control (learned helplessness vs. cognitive fatigue).
Lack of systematic study on the interaction between low social power, powerlessness, and crowding.
Insufficient research on the differential impact of social control policies on high-status vs. low-status individuals in crowded environments.
Lack of empirical confirmation for symbolic interactionist perspective on spatial meanings and roles.
Need for time-series analyses to test temporal and sequential aspects of crowding responses in equilibrium theories.
Conspicuous absence of social position and antecedent conditions in equilibrium models.

moderators.effect: Females tend to respond more positively to crowded conditions than males.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Females show more positive affect, males show more negative affect/aggression.

moderators.effect: High density combined with interpersonal hostility leads to poorer academic performance among dormitory residents.
Individuals experiencing residential crowding selectively withdraw from secondary relationships (strangers, neighbors) but not primary relationships (friends, family).

moderators.variable: Amount of control individuals were given during group tasks
moderators.effect: Perceptions of crowding were affected by the amount of control individuals were given.
Social control mechanisms in crowded groups may favor high-status individuals and disadvantage low-status individuals (e.g., children).
Optimal distances for interactions vary with the level of involvement (e.g., interacting friends vs. non-interacting strangers).

limitations: Early research was often exploratory and atheoretical.
The field has been met with sociological ambivalence and rejection due to perceived irrelevance, weak substantive findings, and nonsociological guiding theories.
Many models (e.g., path models, systems approaches in equilibrium theories) remain interesting yet untested due to lack of data on temporal nature or sequential order of events.
Equilibrium theories can be misleading if improperly used, assuming balanced solutions or ignoring social position.
The concept of personal and perceived control has been taken too far, considering other important social factors too little, especially from a sociological perspective.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Human use of space is a specialized elaboration of culture, influencing communication and social interaction, with concepts like personal space and territoriality being fundamental.
High density or close proximity can lead to increased physiological and psychological arousal, which can be interpreted as negative stress or discomfort.

mechanism_chain.description: Causal mechanism connecting abnormal spatial situations to negative behavioral and psychological responses.

steps.from_construct: close individual distances / territorial invasion / overcrowding
steps.to_construct: perceived loss of personal space / threat / lack of control

steps.from_construct: perceived loss of personal space / threat / lack of control
steps.to_construct: increased physiological arousal / psychological stress / discomfort

steps.from_construct: increased physiological arousal / psychological stress / discomfort
steps.to_construct: aggression / withdrawal / negative affect / reduced performance

instruments_used.name: Self-report questionnaires
instruments_used.construct: psychological stress, discomfort, mood, perceived crowding, privacy
instruments_used.description: Scales measuring subjective experiences and perceptions related to spatial situations.

instruments_used.name: Behavioral observation
instruments_used.construct: aggression, withdrawal, social interaction patterns, gaze aversion, flight distance
instruments_used.description: Direct observation and coding of participant actions and interactions in response to spatial stimuli.

instruments_used.name: Physiological measures
instruments_used.description: Measures such as heart rate, skin conductance, cortisol levels, or blood pressure.
